name: Irfan
voice:
WRITING MECHANICS: Never uses em dashes. No bullet points in posts. No numbered lists. Writes in short punchy single-sentence paragraphs mixed with longer 2-3 sentence paragraphs. Never opens with 'I' — always opens with an observation, a fact, or a scene. Hashtags go at the bottom separated by line breaks, never inline.

LENGTH: Hard limit of 300 words total including hashtags. Target 200 words. Every sentence that does not add new information must be cut. Long posts consistently underperform — the 400-impression posts are short. The 100-impression posts are long. Brevity is not optional.

HASHTAGS: Maximum 3 hashtags. No more. 10 hashtags signals low quality to the algorithm and dilutes the post. Pick the 3 most relevant and stop.

CHARACTERISTIC MOVES: Opens with a counterintuitive or contrarian claim — something that disagrees with the prevailing narrative. The hook that works: a take that makes the reader either nod hard or want to argue. Never opens with a news summary. Always names a specific industry or a specific organisational function — never just 'enterprise' generically. Uses cross-industry contrast as a structural tool: what AI resistance looks like in a telecoms operator is completely different from what it looks like in a facilities management firm, and that contrast is the content. Uses repetition for emphasis sparingly — 'Not in theory. Not in a research paper. In a 30,000-person logistics company, right now.' Ends on a genuine open question that invites a real answer — not rhetorical, not 'is your org ready?', but 'where are you seeing this play out?' or 'what broke first in your organisation when you tried this?' The closing question is an invitation to a conversation, not a test the reader fails.

CREDIBILITY ANCHORS: Cross-industry delivery across telecoms (Vodafone), IT services (Atos, Capgemini), facilities management (Interserve), and construction supply (Travis Perkins). References these not by name-dropping but by saying 'I have watched this exact pattern play out in a telecoms company with 28,000 employees' or 'the conversation in a facilities management firm sounds completely different.' Never claims to be an AI builder or researcher — always the person who was accountable for delivery when the programme hit the real organisation. The gap he owns: most AI advice is written for software companies. Most large organisations are nothing like a software company.

WHAT HE NEVER SAYS: Never uses: delve, it is worth noting, in today's rapidly evolving landscape, game-changer, unlock, leverage, cutting-edge, harness, seamlessly. Never summarises an AI news story — the news is never the post. Never writes a dramatic 'let that land for a second' or 'sit with that' — that register is performative and signals low confidence. Never writes a post that a management consultant who has never delivered a programme could also have written. Never uses more than 3 hashtags.

RELATIONSHIP WITH NEWS: News is a trigger, never the subject. If an AI announcement is relevant, the post is Irfan's take on what it means for a 40,000-person logistics company — not a summary of what Anthropic or IBM said. One sentence maximum on what happened. The rest is the delivery implication.

RELATIONSHIP WITH DATA: Uses one strong number per post maximum. The number is never the point — it is the proof. Leads with the human or organisational insight, drops the data to back it, moves on.

TONE: A senior leader who has delivered too many complex programmes to be impressed by AI hype, and has enough cross-industry scar tissue to know exactly which part of your organisation will be the problem — before you do.
about: 25 years of enterprise technology leadership delivering transformation programmes inside the industries the AI conversation ignores — telecoms (Vodafone), IT services (Atos, Capgemini), facilities management (Interserve), construction supply (Travis Perkins). Not an AI researcher or startup founder. A delivery veteran who has been accountable for programmes that had to survive contact with 30,000-person organisations, legacy infrastructure, and workforces that are mostly non-desk. Based in the United Kingdom, targeting European and Asian business audiences. The gap he writes about: most AI advice is written for software companies. Most large organisations are nothing like a software company — and nobody is writing for their leaders.

pillars.label: The Delivery Lens
pillars.description: What AI transformation actually looks like inside legacy-heavy industries — telecoms, logistics, facilities management, construction supply. Not a consultant's slide deck view. The view from inside, from someone who was accountable when the programme hit the real organisation. The engine of every post here is cross-industry contrast: what AI resistance looks like in a telecoms operator is completely different from a facilities management firm, and that specificity is what nobody else is writing. Audience for this pillar: senior leaders in these industries who have been sold transformation before and are tired of advice written for software companies. Every post must name an industry or a specific organisational context. Never 'enterprise' generically.

pillars.label: Where It Breaks
pillars.description: Not 'adoption gap' generically — the specific layer where AI programmes die. Procurement kills it quietly. Middle management pays lip service and waits it out. The programme sponsor approves the budget then disappears. The governance framework was written by legal without a single conversation with operations. Irfan names the layer, describes the pattern from real delivery experience, and tells you how to spot it before it happens. Every post here names a specific function or role — never vague organisational abstractions. The closing question must name a specific person: 'your procurement director', 'your middle management layer', 'the person accountable when this fails.' This is the pillar that builds his reputation as someone who has seen these patterns across industries and can diagnose them before the post-mortem.

pillars.label: Sharp Takes
pillars.description: Irfan's actual opinions — the ones he would say in a boardroom and stand behind if challenged. A governance trend he thinks is performative theatre. A leadership behaviour he has watched destroy programmes across three industries. A prediction about where enterprise AI is heading that most people are not making yet. A news story that annoyed him because the framing was wrong. No fixed topic, no format rules. The only rule: it must be a real take, not a safe one. Something that will make AI consultants uncomfortable and make senior practitioners who have delivered programmes nod. This is the pillar that drives reach and makes his account feel like a real person with real opinions, not a content machine. Must be active every week.

avoidTopics: AI product reviews or tool comparisons
Technical AI research or model benchmarks
Any post that could have been written by someone who has never delivered a programme
Posts that say 'AI adoption fails culturally' without naming the specific layer or function where it breaks
audienceNotes: Primary: C-suite and senior operations, IT, and transformation leaders at large legacy enterprises — telecoms operators, logistics companies, facilities management firms, construction and manufacturing. These are people who have lived through failed transformation programmes and have been sold the same optimism before. They respect specificity and candour over enthusiasm. Secondary: Asia-Pacific enterprise leaders in the same industries. Thursday posts carry into Asia afternoon engagement window. The goal is reach now, senior role visibility later — every post should make a hiring manager at a large legacy enterprise think 'this person has been in the room I'm in.'

*Topic:* Bank of England reviews AI rules for agentic AI in finance https://share.google/keScNzMkbZJs0CZmf

---
The @BankofEngland is reviewing its AI rules specifically for agentic AI in finance.

Not chatbots. AI that takes autonomous actions, executes decisions, moves money — without a human sign-off in the loop.

Most regulators are still trying to understand ChatGPT. And here the BoE is already naming agentic AI as its own regulatory category.

That tells you something about pace.

I've watched AI adoption move slowly inside large financial services firms — compliance teams nervous, change control heavy, every pilot needing three sign-offs. And that caution made sense when the technology was a text box.

Agentic AI is a different problem entirely. It's not a tool you use. It's a system that acts. The governance model that worked for your chatbot deployment will not hold here.

I don't think most organisations are ready for that shift. Not the technology part. The accountability part. Who owns the decision when the agent made it?

Still working out what that answer looks like in practice. Where are you seeing this land in your organisation?

#EnterpriseAI #TechLeadership #DigitalTransformation

JPMorgan CEO Dimon leads new cross-industry effort to tackle AI risks
By Nupur Anand
August 5, 20263:33 PM GMT+5:30Updated August 6, 2026



U.S. President Donald Trump travels to Pennsylvania for Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit
CEO and Chairman of JPMorgan Chase Jamie Dimon speaks at the Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit at the United States Army War College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, U.S., July 15, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper/File Photo Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab
Summary
Companies
JPMorgan expands critical infrastructure group to increase focus on AI risks
More than 40 firms approached on initiative
AI threats spur new cross-industry collaboration
Dimon says he is a support cast member to get more members to the group
NEW YORK, Aug 5 (Reuters) - JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N), opens new tab CEO Jamie Dimon is urging ​corporate leaders to join a U.S.-focused industry group to address risks posed by AI, as corporate America rapidly adopts the developing technology, two ‌sources familiar with the matter said.
Dimon has personally reached out to CEOs of other large and major regional banks and IT companies to enlist them in the initiative, which he is expanding from a group that JPMorgan helped found called the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure, the sources said.

The ACI and Dimon have also communicated with other prospective members in an effort to schedule calls ​in August to discuss collaboration, the sources said.
The outreach, which started in July, includes more than 40 companies spanning financial services, energy, water, utilities, telecommunications, ​airlines, railroads and other critical infrastructure industries that rely heavily on technology, the sources said. The ACI has not disclosed results ⁠of the effort so far.
Dimon's views on the economy, regulation and technology are closely followed. As head of the largest U.S. bank, he has been among a ​small group of CEOs publicly warning about the risks posed by advanced AI systems.
Advertisement · Scroll to continue


AI RISKS AND SAFEGUARDS
The initiative aims to develop a shared understanding of how AI is ​being used, the risks it poses and the safeguards needed, and to work with the Trump administration on those issues, the sources said. Recent cyberattacks on water systems in Minnesota and other states have increased the need for more information sharing across industries, the sources said.
JPMorgan was a founding member of the ACI, opens new tab alongside Mastercard, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and others. The organization was created to coordinate ​cross-sector resilience planning, share information, and respond to critical infrastructure threats, including cyber, physical and geopolitical risk. The group has a team that is also involved in ​refocusing the ACI and building up the AI effort.
Dimon said in a statement that the ACI leadership had seen the need to prioritize AI "years ago and got critical infrastructure companies working ‌together."

"We are ⁠proud to support this important work," Dimon said.
When asked about the initiative during a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Dimon said ACI's executive chairman Tom Fanning had set up the group a long time ago.
"I am like a support cast member," Dimon said. "This group will help interface with that (the government) and both give advice and take advice from the government."
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Dimon's remarks.
The ACI said in a statement that "at a time of growing cyber ​threats, protecting the systems Americans rely on ​every day requires strong collaboration between ⁠government and critical infrastructure companies."
Mastercard and Berkshire did not respond to requests for comment.
The ACI would serve as an industry response and information-sharing forum, with an intent to work with government officials to identify core AI and technology risks, share information and ​help solve problems as they emerge, the sources said.
Advertisement · Scroll to continue


The group aims to have the revamped ACI fully functional by year-end, ​one of the sources ⁠said.
INDUSTRY, GOVERNMENT EFFORTS
AI concerns have grown rapidly as businesses race to deploy the technology, with regulators and industry leaders warning that AI could also increase cyberattacks and create new vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and financial systems.
Dimon has warned about the risks posed by Anthropic's Mythos AI model, underscoring that access to advanced AI capabilities must be controlled. He said in ⁠July that "you're ​giving ballistic missiles to individuals with Mythos." The ACI effort is separate from an industry effort ​by banks to test Mythos.
The U.S. government has stepped up coordination with industry to manage risks from increasingly powerful AI systems. In July, it launched the Gold Eagle initiative, bringing together AI developers, critical infrastructure operators and ​federal agencies to share information on vulnerabilities discovered by advanced AI models and coordinate fixes.
